KASPER

Act two. Before we build anything: what tracing already gives us, and where it stops.

Source: Ch 14

KASPER

Two words for the rest of the talk.

On the left, one span: the record of one step, like one tool call. It has a name, a start, an end, and labels: facts about the work.

On the right, a trace: every span that shares one trace id. Each span points at its parent, so they form a tree. Read it top down: the customer submits, the agent runs, calls a tool, and the gateway asks the policy service. One request, one story.

Source: Ch 3

KASPER

That tree only holds together if every span carries the same trace id.

Think of a parcel with a tracking number. Every depot scans the label. On the left, every hop kept the label on: one story. On the right, one hop stuck on a new label, and the history splits in two. Nothing errors. You just can't follow it any more.

And agents add a lot of new hops.

Source: Ch 3

KASPER

This is the label: the W3C traceparent header. Version, always zero zero. The trace id, the tracking number, the same on every span. The parent id, replaced at every hop, like a depot stamp. The flags: zero one means sampled.

The news: since the July twenty-eighth MCP spec, SEP-414 puts the same label inside the message, in params underscore meta. So context survives transports with no headers, like stdio. Northstar sends both copies. The gateway reads only the header.

[verify: exact params._meta key names against the 2026-07-28 MCP spec; the slide's JSON is illustrative, not a captured request]

Source: Ch 2, Ch 3

KASPER

Once the trace holds together, the next question is names. You can't query what you can't name.

Semantic conventions are OpenTelemetry's shared dictionary. For "which model", there have been three spellings: llm dot model name from OpenInference, llm dot request model from older OpenLLMetry, and gen underscore ai dot request model, the OpenTelemetry name.

The good news: OpenLLMetry has moved. Since version 0.53.4, in March, it writes the gen_ai names, and its instrumentations now track the OpenTelemetry GenAI conventions. So the dialects are converging. But your platform still holds last year's data, and not every library has moved. A per-model dashboard still has to find all three.

So translate once, in the Collector. The gen_ai normalizer writes one name and keeps the originals beside it, so old dashboards keep working.

[verify: OpenLLMetry gen_ai migration = v0.53.4 (2026-03-29, #3809); latest v0.62.3 (2026-08-10) aligns to GenAI semconv v1.40.0 (#4010). Checked 2026-09-28 against the upstream CHANGELOG]
[verify: gen_ai_normalizer component name, stability level, and the first collector-contrib release that ships it (quoted from the earlier deck as contrib >0.153.0)]

Source: Ch 3; github.com/traceloop/openllmetry CHANGELOG.md

KASPER

So what can the gen_ai names answer? Read across: one, a question an investigator asks; two, the attribute that answers it; three, dimmed rows are the content.

The dark rows are the spec's defaults: kind of step, model, act or stop, tool, conversation.

The dimmed rows are content: what it was told, what it decided, what it asked for, what happened. The most sensitive data, so the spec makes them opt-in. Many libraries capture them anyway: at their defaults, four of seven wrote the model's output. And exactly what an auditor needs. Hold that until Act 4.

[verify: GenAI semconv are all at Development stability in semantic-conventions-genai, which has cut no release; attribute names may move]

Source: Ch 3; Instrumenting AI Agents (Dash0 DevRel, Aug 2026), p. 40

KASPER

And the row that isn't there. A trace proves what happened. Not why. There is no gen_ai dot tool dot call dot reason.

The closest is the model's own output, if content capture is on. In a courtroom, that's a quote from the suspect.

But the platform can tell us why it allowed something, if the platform is the one deciding. That's Act 3.

Source: Ch 3
